translation_en:
“Those above and those below interact, and their intentions are the same.”
Du Jue 杜珏
Associate Examiner Shao, Instructor, comments: Those who study the Book of Changes nowadays often use narrow insights and conjectural explanations to accommodate the principal theme, yet carelessly neglect to investigate the meaning of the Sage’s elucidation of the Changes. This essay alone has a lofty, antique vigor of expression, and its phrasing does not depart from principle. Could its author be someone who devotes himself to classical learning and remains unaltered by prevailing fashions?
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: The exposition of the Changes is pure and clear.
Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: Rich and abundant, it merits attention.
When ruler and ministers associate with one another and their hearts are united, this is what constitutes Peace, or Tai. For when their hearts are united, their Way is also the same, and successful government can be achieved. Once relations between ruler and ministers reach this point, how great must be the peace of human affairs! In antiquity, Fuxi named the hexagram Tai. King Wen appended a judgment describing its success with the words “The small departs; the great arrives.” Our Master further clarified this in his Commentary on the Judgment. His meaning was that Qian, which properly belongs above, occupies the lower position, just as the ruler reaches downward to associate with his ministers; Kun, which properly belongs below, occupies the upper position, just as ministers reach upward to associate with their ruler. When those above associate with those below, the ruler does not rely upon his exalted position, wealth, and rank, but sets his heart solely on honoring virtue and delighting in the Way. In lowering himself, though noble, before those of humble station, he makes splendid the ceremony of receiving them three times; in honoring those below from his position above, he lends weight to the command bestowing three rewards. This is much like the Way of Heaven, which descends to aid those below and shines brightly. When those below associate with those above, ministers do not exalt themselves through withdrawal from the world and cultivation of their own goodness alone, but devote themselves solely to practicing righteousness and bringing the Way into effect. In joining with those outside from within, they express their sincere desire for the beneficial meeting; in honoring those above from their position below, they offer their selfless …

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
躬之節也殆猶地道卑而上行焉夫上下之交
如此吾知叅賛天地阜安民物以立不世之功
者固君之志也而臣之所願欲者亦不外是則
都俞於廟堂之上有孚攣如其利斷金也豈睽
之遇主于巷乎黼黻皇猷琫琫治化以建非常
之業者固臣之志也而君之所好尚者亦不出
此則賡歌於殿陛之閒厥孚交如其臭如蘭也
豈坎之納約自牖乎是則際明良之嘉會成治
世之宏圖猗歟盛哉大抵君臣相遇非偶然者
要皆氣數之盛以致之也故孔子傳泰卦之彖
而以君臣際會為言則義文名卦繫辭之旨蓋
然於言意之表而以見易之關於天下治道者
非淺淺也豈直為象數之書乎此又學易者所
當致意焉
===
夫易聖人之所以極深而研幾也
夏廷芝
同考試官教諭邵　批〔題本平易作者多牽强上文入講草率可厭此篇體認明白辭氣老健而〕〔一結尤有精采宜〕
punctuated:
躬之節也，殆猶地道卑而上行焉。夫上下之交如此，吾知叅賛天地、阜安民物以立不世之功者，固君之志也，而臣之所願欲者亦不外是。則都俞於廟堂之上，有孚攣如，其利斷金也，豈睽之遇主于巷乎？黼黻皇猷、琫琫治化以建非常之業者，固臣之志也，而君之所好尚者亦不出此。則賡歌於殿陛之閒，厥孚交如，其臭如蘭也，豈坎之納約自牖乎？是則際明良之嘉會，成治世之宏圖，猗歟盛哉！大抵君臣相遇，非偶然者，要皆氣數之盛以致之也。故孔子傳泰卦之彖，而以君臣際會為言，則義文名卦繫辭之旨，蓋然於言意之表，而以見《易》之關於天下治道者非淺淺也，豈直為象數之書乎？此又學《易》者所當致意焉。

夫《易》，聖人之所以極深而研幾也。
夏廷芝

translation_en:
…the integrity of selfless service, much as the way of earth lies low yet moves upward. When those above and below associate in this fashion, I know that assisting Heaven and Earth, bringing prosperity and peace to the people and all creatures, and thereby establishing achievements unmatched in an age are indeed the ruler’s aspirations; what his ministers desire goes no further than this. Thus, in their exchanges of approval in the court, they are bound together by sincerity, their unity sharp enough to cut metal. How could this be merely the encounter with one’s lord in a lane described in Kui, the hexagram of Opposition? To embellish imperial plans and advance [?] the transforming influence of government, thereby establishing extraordinary accomplishments, is indeed the ministers’ aspiration; what the ruler esteems likewise goes no further than this. Thus, as they exchange songs within the palace, their sincerity is mutual and its fragrance is like orchids. How could this be merely the presentation of simple offerings through a window described in Kan, the hexagram of the Abyss? This is the felicitous meeting of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers, bringing to fruition the grand design of a well-governed age. Ah, how splendid!

Generally speaking, the meeting of ruler and ministers is no chance occurrence: ultimately, it is brought about by the flourishing of cosmic forces and destiny. Thus, when Confucius commented on the Judgment of the hexagram Tai, Peace, he spoke of the meeting of ruler and ministers. The intent with which Fuxi and King Wen [?] named the hexagrams and appended their statements is thereby apparent [?] beyond the surface of words and meanings. This reveals that the Changes has no shallow connection with the principles of governing the world. Could it be merely a book of images and numbers? This, too, deserves the attention of those who study the Changes.

“The Changes is that by which the sages plumb the depths and investigate the incipient workings of things.”
Xia Tingzhi

考試官教諭張 批〔說理之文自合如此〕
考試官教諭李 批〔講極研字不類衆作〕
論易之爲書乃聖人所以闡夫理之妙焉蓋理
莫妙於深與幾也然非聖人之作易其孰能極
之研之也哉昔大傳論易有聖人之道四焉至
此謂夫易有辭也有占也而辭占爲天下之至
精易有象也有變也而象變爲天下之至變易
之爲書如此果何爲者哉彼如幽明之故死生
===
之說與夫鬼神屈信之機皆理之至深而難測
者也易之辭占莫不推而極之焉蓋必不假乎
料想臆度之私有以究竟其本原發用之輿殆
猶鑑之空而毫髮畢照也若然則理之深者在
易而通志之體立矣易非聖人之所以極深者
乎如吉凶之未至悔吝之將萌與夫失得憂虞
之象皆理之至幾而難見者也易之象變莫不
研而審之焉蓋必無事乎識緯術數之學有以
詳察其端倪联兆之微殆猶衡之平而錙銖不
punctuated:
得之，寧不歆羨？
考試官教諭張批〔說理之文自合如此〕
考試官教諭李批〔講極研字不類衆作〕
論《易》之爲書，乃聖人所以闡夫理之妙焉。蓋理莫妙於深與幾也，然非聖人之作《易》，其孰能極之、研之也哉？昔《大傳》論《易》，有聖人之道四焉。至此謂夫《易》有辭也，有占也，而辭占爲天下之至精；《易》有象也，有變也，而象變爲天下之至變。《易》之爲書如此，果何爲者哉？彼如幽明之故、死生之說，與夫鬼神屈信之機，皆理之至深而難測者也。《易》之辭占，莫不推而極之焉。蓋必不假乎料想臆度之私，有以究竟其本原發用之輿，殆猶鑑之空而毫髮畢照也。若然，則理之深者在《易》，而通志之體立矣。《易》非聖人之所以極深者乎？如吉凶之未至、悔吝之將萌，與夫失得憂虞之象，皆理之至幾而難見者也。《易》之象變，莫不研而審之焉。蓋必無事乎識緯術數之學，有以詳察其端倪联兆之微，殆猶衡之平而錙銖不
translation_en:
…attaining it—how could one fail to admire and envy him?

Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: 〔Writing that expounds principle should indeed be like this.〕

Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: 〔The exposition of the words “fathom” and “investigate” differs from the other compositions.〕

To discuss the Changes as a book: it is the means by which the sages elucidate the subtleties of principle. Nothing in principle is subtler than its depths and its incipient tendencies. Yet had the sages not composed the Changes, who could have fathomed those depths and investigated those tendencies? Earlier, the Great Commentary, discussing the Changes, spoke of four ways of the sages within it. At this point it says that the Changes has statements and divinations, and these are the most refined things under Heaven; it has images and transformations, and these are the most changeful things under Heaven. Such being the Changes as a book, what, indeed, does it accomplish?

Consider the causes of the hidden and the manifest, the explanations of death and life, and the workings of the contraction and expansion of ghosts and spirits: these are the deepest and most unfathomable aspects of principle. The statements and divinations of the Changes trace and fathom them all. Without recourse to private conjecture or speculation, they thoroughly explore principle’s source and its manifestation in operation [?], much as an unclouded mirror reflects every hair. Thus the depths of principle reside in the Changes, and the foundation for comprehending intentions is established. Is the Changes not the means by which the sages fathom the depths?

Consider good and ill fortune before they arrive, regret and humiliation as they begin to emerge, and the signs of loss and gain, anxiety and apprehension: these are the most incipient and least perceptible aspects of principle. The images and transformations of the Changes investigate and scrutinize them all. Without resorting to the study of apocryphal writings [?] or divinatory techniques, they closely examine the subtle beginnings and portents [?], much as a level balance allows not even the smallest weight to…

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
奧也若然則理之幾者在易而成務之體具矣
易非聖人之所以研幾者乎是則辭占象變信
乎為聖人之道而人之所當尚者歟抑嘗論之
人惟心之精斯能極深以通志人惟心之變斯
能研幾以成務然則易之精變即聖人之心虛
靈也而其所極之深所研之幾即聖人心中所
具之理也是則易乃無言之聖人聖人乃有言
之易而此章首尾皆曰易有聖人之道良有以
夫
===
書
惟暨乃僚罔不同心以匡乃辟
王崇獻
同考試官訓導李 批〔商書篇甚多此中作者類能 〕
〔言之但浮詞可厭獨此篇理明意足且寫出高宗重望傅說之〕
〔意殆盡異日出為〕
〔世用其必有以仰體〕
〔君上之心者矣〕
同考試官教諭王 批〔本題作者率多泛雜鮮理惟〕
punctuated:
奧也。若然，則理之幾者在易，而成務之體具矣。易非聖人之所以研幾者乎？是則辭占象變，信乎為聖人之道，而人之所當尚者歟？抑嘗論之：人惟心之精，斯能極深以通志；人惟心之變，斯能研幾以成務。然則易之精變，即聖人之心虛靈也；而其所極之深、所研之幾，即聖人心中所具之理也。是則易乃無言之聖人，聖人乃有言之易，而此章首尾皆曰「易有聖人之道」，良有以夫！

書
惟暨乃僚，罔不同心，以匡乃辟。
王崇獻
同考試官訓導李批〔商書篇甚多，此中作者類能〕〔言之，但浮詞可厭。獨此篇理明意足，且寫出高宗重望傅說之〕〔意殆盡。異日出為〕〔世用，其必有以仰體〕〔君上之心者矣。〕
同考試官教諭王批〔本題作者率多泛雜鮮理，惟〕
translation_en:
…[?]. If this is so, the incipient subtleties of principle reside in the Changes, and the foundation for accomplishing affairs is complete. Is not the Changes the means by which the sages investigate these subtleties? Thus its statements, prognostications, images, and transformations surely constitute the way of the sages and are what people ought to esteem. Yet I have considered this: only through the refinement of the mind can a person fathom the depths and comprehend intentions; only through the mind’s adaptability can a person investigate incipient subtleties and accomplish affairs. Thus the refinement and transformations of the Changes are the openness and numinous awareness of the sage’s mind; the depths it fathoms and the subtleties it investigates are the principles inherent in that mind. The Changes is therefore a sage without speech, and the sage is the Changes endowed with speech. There is indeed good reason why both the beginning and the end of this chapter say, “The Changes contains the way of the sages”!

Book of Documents
“You and your colleagues must all be of one mind in assisting your ruler.”
Wang Chongxian

Associate Examiner Li, Assistant Instructor, comments: 〔There are many essays on the Documents of Shang, and the writers here can generally〕〔discuss them, but their empty verbiage is wearisome. This essay alone makes its principles clear and fully develops its meaning; moreover, it conveys almost completely the〕〔great expectations that Gaozong placed upon Fu Yue. When its author comes forth〕〔to serve the world in the future, he will surely be able reverently to apprehend〕〔the mind of his sovereign.〕

Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔Most writers on this topic are vague and miscellaneous, with little coherent reasoning. Only…〕

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
是篇純詞老健說理詳明蓋嘗究心於壁經而得其妙者歟錄之
考試官教諭張　批〔深得命相之旨〕
考試官教諭李　批〔理明詞順〕
恊人已之心而盡輔弼之道此賢王之望大臣
也蓋一已聰明有限而衆人聞見無窮大臣之
責必合衆人之心以輔君焉昔高宗命說之意
若曰以已事君固相職之當然以人事君尤相
職之當盡彼納誨輔德我之望於爾者固切矣
然爾之下有卿士焉皆共天位而食天祿者誰
===
無輔君之心乎啓心沃心我之資於汝者固至
矣然爾之下有衆職焉皆治天民而理天事者
孰無正君之責乎汝必倡而導之使職之大者
此心職之小者此心而臣救其君之失合大小
而同符不判其心於爾我也統而率之使職之
尊者此志職之卑者此志而弼正其君之非合
尊卑而一致不隔其心於形骸也彬彬乎各操
夫堯舜其君之心務使君之德純一不二足以
匹休先世而表正乎萬邦焉濟濟乎各秉夫左
punctuated:
是篇純詞老健，說理詳明，蓋嘗究心於壁經而得其妙者歟？錄之。
考試官教諭張，批〔深得命相之旨〕。
考試官教諭李，批〔理明詞順〕。
恊人已之心而盡輔弼之道，此賢王之望大臣也。蓋一已聰明有限，而衆人聞見無窮。大臣之責，必合衆人之心以輔君焉。昔高宗命說之意，若曰：「以已事君，固相職之當然；以人事君，尤相職之當盡。彼納誨輔德，我之望於爾者固切矣。然爾之下有卿士焉，皆共天位而食天祿者，誰無輔君之心乎？啓心沃心，我之資於汝者固至矣。然爾之下有衆職焉，皆治天民而理天事者，孰無正君之責乎？汝必倡而導之，使職之大者此心，職之小者此心，而臣救其君之失，合大小而同符，不判其心於爾我也。統而率之，使職之尊者此志，職之卑者此志，而弼正其君之非，合尊卑而一致，不隔其心於形骸也。彬彬乎，各操夫堯舜其君之心，務使君之德純一不二，足以匹休先世而表正乎萬邦焉。濟濟乎，各秉夫左
translation_en:
…this essay’s refined language is mature and vigorous, and its explanation of principle is detailed and clear. Surely its author has carefully studied the classic recovered from the wall and grasped its subtleties? Let it be included.
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “It profoundly grasps the intent behind appointing a chief minister.”
Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “The reasoning is clear and the language flows smoothly.”
To harmonize the minds of others with one’s own and fully discharge the duty of assisting and correcting the ruler: this is what a worthy king expects of his great ministers. One person’s intelligence is limited, whereas the knowledge and experience of the multitude are inexhaustible. A great minister’s responsibility therefore requires him to unite the minds of all in assisting the ruler.
The intent of Gaozong’s charge to Fu Yue in former times was as though he had said: “Serving the ruler through your own efforts is certainly an inherent duty of the chief minister; serving him through the efforts of others is all the more a duty that the chief minister must fulfill. My expectations that you offer instruction and foster my virtue are indeed earnest. Yet beneath you are ministers and officers, all sharing the positions bestowed by Heaven and enjoying Heaven’s emoluments. Who among them lacks the desire to assist the ruler? In opening and nourishing my mind, my reliance upon you is indeed complete. Yet beneath you are the holders of the various offices, all governing Heaven’s people and managing Heaven’s affairs. Who among them has no responsibility to rectify the ruler?
“You must take the initiative and guide them, so that those with great responsibilities and those with small responsibilities share this same purpose. Thus, as ministers remedy their ruler’s failings, those in greater and lesser offices will act in accord, without dividing their intentions into yours and mine. You must unite and lead them, so that those of high rank and those of low rank share this same aspiration. Thus, as they assist and correct their ruler’s errors, those of high and low rank will act as one, without allowing their separate persons to keep their minds apart. With cultivated bearing, let each cherish the purpose of making his ruler a Yao or a Shun, striving to make the ruler’s virtue pure and undivided, sufficient to equal the glory of earlier generations and serve as a model for the myriad states. With dignified bearing, let each hold fast to the resolve to assist [?] …

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
石嚴辟之志務使君之心至誠無偽足以追配
前人而作則乎天下焉夫如是則能合衆人之
善以成輔君之功何患相業有不盡哉抑論之
泰山不辭土壤故能成其大河海不擇細流故
能成其深人君不資衆善何以成其德乎高宗
有見於此故拳拳於說言之下文說復之曰后
從諫則聖臣不命其承有以見高宗之心惟恐
進諫之不多傅說之意惟恐從諫之不切君明
臣良更相戒飭此高宗所以爲商令王而無愧
於湯傅說所以爲商賢佐而無愧於尹也歟
爾克敬典在德時乃罔不變允升于大猷
張諾
同考試官訓導李　批〔此作以身教立說深得麻王命君陳端本化殺之意且文有典則氣也雄渾其東南之佳士也高爲何泰〕
同考試官教諭王　批〔體認真切發揮詳盡風簷寸晷之下能有此作非素於講貫而有得者不能本房優選舍子其誰〕
punctuated:
石嚴辟之志，務使君之心至誠無偽，足以追配前人而作則乎天下焉。夫如是，則能合衆人之善以成輔君之功，何患相業有不盡哉？抑論之，泰山不辭土壤，故能成其大；河海不擇細流，故能成其深。人君不資衆善，何以成其德乎？高宗有見於此，故拳拳於說。言之下文，說復之曰：「后從諫則聖，臣不命其承。」有以見高宗之心，惟恐進諫之不多；傅說之意，惟恐從諫之不切。君明臣良，更相戒飭，此高宗所以爲商令王而無愧於湯，傅說所以爲商賢佐而無愧於尹也歟！

爾克敬典在德，時乃罔不變，允升于大猷。
張諾

同考試官訓導李　批〔此作以身教立說，深得麻王命君陳端本化殺之意，且文有典則，氣也雄渾，其東南之佳士也。高爲何泰〕
同考試官教諭王　批〔體認真切，發揮詳盡。風簷寸晷之下，能有此作，非素於講貫而有得者不能。本房優選，舍子其誰？〕
translation_en:
…the resolve to assist and revere the sovereign [?], striving to make the ruler’s heart utterly sincere and free of falsehood, worthy of matching his predecessors and serving as a model for all under Heaven. In this way, one can unite the virtues of many to accomplish the work of assisting the ruler. Why worry that the duties of a chief minister might remain unfulfilled? To discuss this further: Mount Tai does not reject soil, and thus achieves its greatness; rivers and seas do not discriminate against small streams, and thus achieve their depth. Unless a ruler draws upon the virtues of many, how can he perfect his own virtue? Gaozong understood this, and therefore earnestly pressed his charge upon Yue. In the ensuing passage, Yue replied: “When the sovereign follows remonstrance, he becomes a sage; his servants carry out his wishes without awaiting commands.” This shows that Gaozong feared only that too few would offer remonstrance, while Fu Yue feared only that remonstrance would not be followed wholeheartedly. An enlightened ruler and a worthy minister admonished and encouraged one another. Was this not why Gaozong became an excellent king of Shang, worthy of Tang, and Fu Yue a worthy minister of Shang, worthy of Yi Yin?

“If you can reverently uphold the constant norms, grounding yourself in virtue, then none will fail to be transformed, and they will truly advance to the Great Way.”
Zhang Nuo

Associate Examiner Li, Assistant Instructor, comments: 〔This composition bases its argument on teaching by personal example. It deeply grasps the intention of King Ma [?] in charging Jun Chen to rectify the root and transform severity [?]. Moreover, its writing follows classical standards, and its force is vigorous and full. He is an outstanding scholar of the southeast. The concluding phrase, 高爲何泰, is unclear [?].〕
Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔His understanding is genuine and precise, and his exposition thorough and exhaustive. To produce such a composition beneath the wind-swept eaves, in the brief time allotted, would be impossible for anyone who had not long studied and discussed these matters and gained insight into them. For the outstanding selection from this examining section, whom could we choose but you?〕

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭張　批〔得經義程度〕
考試官教諭李　批〔深合題意〕
惟大臣能謹其身教則有以化乎民而善乎俗
矣蓋民之於上固不從其令而從其好大臣能
謹其所好而以身爲教焉則民之化俗之善有
出於必然者矣昔成王命君陳往治東郊而言
及乎此謂夫訓告之切孰若身教之難忘誦說
之勤不如薰炙之易入往治殷民惟自爾身始
焉是故父子君臣之道常道也是道也爾有之
===
殷民未染惡之先亦有之殆必兢兢焉立爾民
極父子盡其親君臣盡其義于以得是道而著
之於躬行無表裏之相違可也兄弟夫婦朋友
之理常理也是理也爾具之殷民未有遷之前
亦具之殆必業業焉立爾民則長幼盡其序夫
婦盡其別朋友盡其信于以得是理而見之於
實踐無內外之相背可也如是則能盡其厚而
謹其所好矣吾知實之感人捷於桴鼓彼殷之
頑民以蕩凌德向固弗若于汝政矣今則得於
punctuated:
考試官教諭張批〔得經義程度。〕
考試官教諭李批〔深合題意。〕
惟大臣能謹其身教，則有以化乎民而善乎俗矣。蓋民之於上，固不從其令而從其好。大臣能謹其所好而以身爲教焉，則民之化、俗之善，有出於必然者矣。昔成王命君陳往治東郊，而言及乎此，謂夫訓告之切，孰若身教之難忘？誦說之勤，不如薰炙之易入。往治殷民，惟自爾身始焉。是故父子君臣之道，常道也。是道也，爾有之，殷民未染惡之先亦有之。殆必兢兢焉，立爾民極，父子盡其親，君臣盡其義，于以得是道而著之於躬行，無表裏之相違，可也。兄弟夫婦朋友之理，常理也。是理也，爾具之，殷民未有遷之前亦具之。殆必業業焉，立爾民則，長幼盡其序，夫婦盡其別，朋友盡其信，于以得是理而見之於實踐，無內外之相背，可也。如是，則能盡其厚而謹其所好矣。吾知實之感人，捷於桴鼓。彼殷之頑民，以蕩凌德，向固弗若于汝政矣，今則得於
translation_en:
Examiner Zhang, an Instructor, comments: 〔Meets the standards for interpreting the Classics.〕
Examiner Li, an Instructor, comments: 〔Closely accords with the meaning of the topic.〕
Only when a great minister carefully attends to teaching by personal example can he transform the people and improve their customs. For in their relations with those above them, the people follow not their commands but their preferences. If a great minister is careful about what he favors and teaches through his own conduct, the transformation of the people and the improvement of their customs will necessarily follow.
When King Cheng commanded Jun Chen to go and govern the eastern suburbs, he spoke of this very matter. His meaning was this: however earnest admonitions may be, how can they compare with the unforgettable force of personal example? Diligent recitation and explanation are less readily absorbed than the influence of close personal contact. In going to govern the people of Yin, begin with your own person. Thus, the Way governing fathers and sons, rulers and ministers, is the constant Way. You possess this Way, and the people of Yin also possessed it before they were tainted by evil. You must therefore act with vigilant care to establish yourself as the highest model for your people. Let fathers and sons fully realize their affection, and rulers and ministers their righteousness. In this way, grasp this Way and make it manifest in your own conduct, allowing no discrepancy between outward appearance and inward reality.
The principles governing brothers, husbands and wives, and friends are constant principles. You are endowed with these principles, and the people of Yin were likewise endowed with them before they changed. You must therefore act with scrupulous care to establish yourself as the standard for your people. Let elders and juniors fully observe their proper order, husbands and wives their distinctions, and friends their trustworthiness. In this way, grasp these principles and reveal them in practice, allowing no conflict between what is within and what is without. By doing so, you will fully realize your moral generosity and be careful about what you favor.
I know that the influence of genuine conduct upon others is swifter than a drum’s response to the drumstick. Those obstinate people of Yin, who used their unrestrained behavior to affront virtue, formerly would indeed not comply with your governance. Now, however, they gain from …

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
觀感莫不舍其舊而從乎新怙侈滅義昔固弗
化于汝訓矣今則有所企慕莫不去其惡而遷
於善親義之理藹然於比屋之間而與古之於
變時雍同一大道之時也序別信之道秩然於
閭閻之下而與古之四方風動同一昇平之世
也如是則民亦歸於厚而從其所好矣是則世
道之善而善於殷民向化之日殷民之化而化
於君陳身教之餘端本澄源責其有所歸乎柳
考有周之世文武作之於前成王述之於後其
所以為殷民安排而布置者蓋無不周矣而猶
洶洶不靖者何哉蓋殷之頑民染紂之惡深被
周之化淺加之三監為周至親而又叛武庚為
殷之後而被誅而有以動搖其心耳斯時也若
無周公君陳之徒相繼撫之則周之天下未可
知也然亦殷民之幸耳若在強楚之時則席卷
而坑之矣又何暇於多誥哉嗚呼此周家所以
為仁厚之至而享國八百年也歟
詩
punctuated:
觀感，莫不舍其舊而從乎新。怙侈滅義，昔固弗化于汝訓矣；今則有所企慕，莫不去其惡而遷於善。親義之理藹然於比屋之間，而與古之於變時雍同一大道之時也；序別信之道秩然於閭閻之下，而與古之四方風動同一昇平之世也。如是，則民亦歸於厚而從其所好矣。是則世道之善，而善於殷民向化之日；殷民之化，而化於君陳身教之餘。端本澄源，責其有所歸乎！
柳考有周之世，文武作之於前，成王述之於後，其所以為殷民安排而布置者，蓋無不周矣。而猶洶洶不靖者，何哉？蓋殷之頑民染紂之惡深，被周之化淺，加之三監為周至親而又叛，武庚為殷之後而被誅，而有以動搖其心耳。斯時也，若無周公、君陳之徒相繼撫之，則周之天下未可知也。然亦殷民之幸耳。若在強楚之時，則席卷而坑之矣，又何暇於多誥哉！嗚呼！此周家所以為仁厚之至而享國八百年也歟！
詩
translation_en:
…through observing your example and being moved by it, all abandon their old ways and follow the new. Clinging to extravagance and destroying righteousness, they formerly remained unchanged by your instruction; now they have something to admire and aspire to, and all abandon their evil ways and turn toward goodness. The principles of familial affection and righteousness flourish among neighboring households, sharing in that same age of the Great Way in antiquity when the people were transformed and brought into harmony. The ways of precedence, distinction, and trustworthiness prevail in orderly fashion throughout the neighborhoods, sharing in that same peaceful age in antiquity when the four quarters stirred as if moved by the wind. Thus the people, too, return to moral generosity and follow what their ruler cherishes. The moral order of the world becomes good on the day when the people of Yin turn toward transformation; the transformation of the people of Yin follows from Jun Chen’s teaching through personal example. To rectify the root and cleanse the source—is this not to place responsibility where it belongs?
Considering [?] the age of Zhou, Kings Wen and Wu initiated the undertaking, and King Cheng carried it on afterward. Their arrangements and provisions for the people of Yin were surely thorough in every respect. Why, then, did unrest and turmoil persist? The recalcitrant people of Yin were deeply steeped in King Zhou’s wickedness and only lightly touched by Zhou’s transforming influence. Moreover, the Three Supervisors, though close kinsmen of the Zhou royal house, had rebelled, while Wu Geng, the heir of Yin, had been executed. These events unsettled their hearts. At that time, had men such as the Duke of Zhou and Jun Chen not successively pacified them, the fate of Zhou’s realm would have been uncertain. Yet this was also good fortune for the people of Yin. Had they lived in the time of powerful Chu, they would have been swept away and buried in pits. What leisure would there have been for so many proclamations? Alas! Was this not why the house of Zhou reached the utmost in benevolence and generosity and held its realm for eight hundred years?
Book of Odes

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
威儀抑抑德音秩秩無怨無惡率由羣匹
受福無疆四方之綱之綱之紀燕及朋友
百辟卿士媚于天子不解于位民之攸塈
趙睿
同考試官訓導楊　批〔題本正大作者多將泛詞〕
〔體貼文明惟此篇鋪張明白詞語春容深得詩人稱願之意〕
同考試官教諭朱　批〔詞氣溫雅說出公尸稱願王〕
〔讀之令人躍然是宜錄出〕
〔者子孫之意殆無餘蘊佳作也〕
===
考試官教諭張　批〔理教明白而詞足以發之可〕
考試官教諭李　批〔理明詞健〕
〔嘉可嘉〕
詩人稱願王者之子孫也既欲其立治本而獲
福以統治尤欲其垂治休而得臣以願治盖脩
德任賢人君獲福統治之大本也然非垂治休
而得臣以願之又豈能久福以保治哉公尸答
君而稱願其子孫如此忠愛之意至矣昔公尸
之所以答鳬鷖此則稱願其子孫謂夫人君之
punctuated:
威儀抑抑，德音秩秩，無怨無惡，率由羣匹。受福無疆，四方之綱。之綱之紀，燕及朋友。百辟卿士，媚于天子，不解于位，民之攸塈。
趙睿。
同考試官訓導楊批〔題本正大，作者多將泛詞〕〔體貼文明，惟此篇鋪張明白，詞語春容，深得詩人稱願之意。〕
同考試官教諭朱批〔詞氣溫雅，說出公尸稱願王〕〔讀之令人躍然，是宜錄出。〕〔者子孫之意，殆無餘蘊，佳作也。〕
考試官教諭張批〔理教明白，而詞足以發之，可〕
考試官教諭李批〔理明詞健。〕〔嘉可嘉。〕
詩人稱願王者之子孫也。既欲其立治本而獲福以統治，尤欲其垂治休而得臣以願治。盖脩德任賢，人君獲福統治之大本也。然非垂治休而得臣以願之，又豈能久福以保治哉？公尸答君而稱願其子孫如此，忠愛之意至矣。昔公尸之所以答鳬鷖，此則稱願其子孫，謂夫人君之
translation_en:
“Your bearing is dignified; your virtuous reputation is well ordered. Without resentment or hatred, you follow your worthy companions. You receive blessings without limit and are the guiding cord of the four quarters. Their guiding cord and their ordering thread, you extend tranquillity to your friends. The many lords, ministers, and officers love the Son of Heaven. Unflagging in their posts, they are those in whom the people find rest.”
Zhao Rui.
Associate Examiner Yang, Assistant Instructor, comments: “The topic is fundamentally upright and grand. Most writers apply vague language to elucidate its wording [?]. This essay alone develops it clearly, with language as gracious as spring, profoundly capturing the poet’s intent in offering praise and good wishes.”
Associate Examiner Zhu, Instructor, comments: “The language and tone are gentle and refined. It expresses almost exhaustively the intent of the ducal impersonator of the ancestral spirit in praising and wishing well to the king’s descendants. An excellent composition.” An intervening annotation reads: “Reading it makes one leap with delight. It certainly deserves inclusion.”
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “The principles and teaching [?] are clear, and the language adequately brings them out. Admirable, admirable!” [The final words of this comment appear after Li’s comment in the transcription.]
Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “Clear reasoning and vigorous language.”
The poet praises and offers good wishes to the king’s descendants. He wishes them to establish the foundation of government and receive blessings through which to govern; still more, he wishes them to extend the beneficence of their rule and obtain ministers with whom to aspire to good government [?]. For cultivating virtue and employing worthy men are the great foundations upon which a ruler receives blessings and governs. Yet unless he extends the beneficence of his rule and obtains ministers to wish for this [?], how can he perpetuate his blessings and preserve good government? The ducal impersonator of the ancestral spirit responds to the ruler and thus praises and wishes well to his descendants: his loyalty and affection are consummate indeed. title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
願莫大乎福祿之盛福祿之盛莫大乎子孫之
賢吾願吾王之子孫德之見於威儀者抑抑乎
其甚容德之形於聲譽者秩秩乎其有常威儀
美矣又能無私怨焉以任乎衆賢而賢者在位
聲譽隆矣又能無私惡焉以由乎羣匹而能者
在職是以能受無疆之福榮膺寶曆乘六龍以
御天四方之廣一在其統括也享無窮之福寵
握瑶圖居九重以凝命萬邦之大一在其綱維
也夫惟能綱乎四方也則庶績咸熙而君師之
===
道盡臣下不賴之以安乎能紀乎四方也則庶
事惟康而治理之功成朋友不賴之以燕乎是
以外而百辟媚茲愛吾天子者同一心内而卿
士媚而戴吾元后者同一志惟欲時脩德時任
賢綱焉常張永受無疆之福于以措斯民於康
乂而同沾垂拱之休可也奚但安及臣下而已
哉時任賢時脩德紀焉常理永享無窮之休于
以撫羣生於嘉靖而同被無為之化可也豈但
燕及朋友而已哉吁統治於脩德任賢之餘保
punctuated: 願莫大乎福祿之盛，福祿之盛莫大乎子孫之賢。吾願吾王之子孫，德之見於威儀者，抑抑乎其甚容；德之形於聲譽者，秩秩乎其有常。威儀美矣，又能無私怨焉，以任乎衆賢，而賢者在位；聲譽隆矣，又能無私惡焉，以由乎羣匹，而能者在職。是以能受無疆之福，榮膺寶曆，乘六龍以御天，四方之廣，一在其統括也；享無窮之福，寵握瑶圖，居九重以凝命，萬邦之大，一在其綱維也。夫惟能綱乎四方也，則庶績咸熙，而君師之道盡，臣下不賴之以安乎？能紀乎四方也，則庶事惟康，而治理之功成，朋友不賴之以燕乎？是以外而百辟媚茲，愛吾天子者同一心；内而卿士媚而，戴吾元后者同一志。惟欲時脩德，時任賢，綱焉常張，永受無疆之福，于以措斯民於康乂，而同沾垂拱之休可也，奚但安及臣下而已哉？時任賢，時脩德，紀焉常理，永享無窮之休，于以撫羣生於嘉靖，而同被無為之化可也，豈但燕及朋友而已哉？吁！統治於脩德任賢之餘，保
translation_en:
…no wish is greater than abundant blessings and emoluments, and no abundance of blessings and emoluments is greater than having worthy descendants. I wish that, among our king’s descendants, virtue manifested in their dignified bearing may be restrained and richly gracious, and virtue expressed in their reputation may be orderly and constant. With their bearing already admirable, may they also harbor no private resentments, so that they employ the many worthy men and the worthy occupy positions of authority. With their reputation already exalted, may they also harbor no private aversions, so that they make use of their associates and the capable hold office. Thus they can receive boundless blessings, gloriously inherit the precious imperial succession, and ride the six dragons to govern Heaven: the vast reaches of the four quarters will all fall within their command. They can enjoy inexhaustible blessings, graciously entrusted with the jade chart of sovereignty, and dwell within the ninefold palace to secure the Mandate: the multitude of states will all be held together by their governance.

Precisely because they can hold the four quarters together, every achievement will flourish and the Way of ruler and teacher will be fully realized. Will their subjects not depend upon them for peace? Because they can order the four quarters, all affairs will proceed well and the work of government will be accomplished. Will their friends not depend upon them for repose? Thus, outside the court, the many lords cherish them, and those who love our Son of Heaven share one heart; within the court, the ministers cherish them, and those who uphold our sovereign share one purpose. Their sole desire is that he continually cultivate virtue and employ worthy men, keeping the governing cords always taut and forever receiving boundless blessings. Thereby he may establish the people in peace and good order, so that all alike partake of the blessings of rule with folded hands. Why should the peace he brings extend only to his subjects? By continually employing worthy men and cultivating virtue, keeping the ordering threads always straight and forever enjoying inexhaustible blessings, he may nurture all living people in felicity and tranquility, so that all alike receive the transforming influence of effortless rule. Why should the repose he brings extend only to his friends? Ah! Having brought all under orderly rule through cultivating virtue and employing worthy men, to preserve…

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
治於安臣致愛之後公尸荅君而稱願其子孫
之賢如此何其忠愛之至哉大抵富貴尊榮一
身之福子孫之賢無疆之福故禹得啓賢而夏
祚以永文得武聖而周業以昌既醉之詩則曰
孝子不匱永錫爾類有駜之頌則曰君子有穀
詒孫子是子孫之賢誠為王者之盛福也今公
尸荅君而願其子孫之賢如此其亦有見於此
歟
===
天命降監下民有嚴
同考試官訓導楊　批〔此題傳註最明白作者鮮能體認　文精人往以高宗敬天畏民之講殊失本旨見理明而措詞當者〕
無踰此篇
同考試官教諭朱　批〔題意天命在民正見民之所　以可畏此作體貼明白措詞整潔故録以式後學〕
考試官教諭張　批〔題意正如此他作無出其右者〕
考試官教諭李　批〔典雅可取〕
詩人即天命之有在乎民而見其民為可畏焉
punctuated:
治於安臣致愛之後，公尸荅君而稱願其子孫之賢如此，何其忠愛之至哉！大抵富貴尊榮，一身之福；子孫之賢，無疆之福。故禹得啓賢而夏祚以永，文得武聖而周業以昌。《既醉》之詩則曰：「孝子不匱，永錫爾類。」《有駜》之頌則曰：「君子有穀，詒孫子。」是子孫之賢，誠為王者之盛福也。今公尸荅君而願其子孫之賢如此，其亦有見於此歟？

天命降監，下民有嚴。

同考試官訓導楊　批〔此題傳註最明白，作者鮮能體認。文精人往以高宗敬天畏民之講，殊失本旨。見理明而措詞當者〕無踰此篇。

同考試官教諭朱　批〔題意天命在民，正見民之所　以可畏。此作體貼明白，措詞整潔，故録以式後學。〕

考試官教諭張　批〔題意正如此，他作無出其右者。〕

考試官教諭李　批〔典雅可取。〕

詩人即天命之有在乎民，而見其民為可畏焉。
translation_en:
…order, after bringing peace to his ministers and winning their affection. The ritual impersonator responds to the ruler by expressing such wishes for the worthiness of his descendants: how consummate his loyalty and affection! Wealth, rank, honor, and glory are blessings for one lifetime; worthy descendants are blessings without limit. Thus Yu had the worthy Qi, and the Xia dynasty endured; King Wen had the sage King Wu, and the enterprise of Zhou flourished. The poem “Already Drunk” (Ji zui) says: “Filial sons shall never fail; blessings shall forever be bestowed upon your kind.” The hymn “The Stout Horses” (You bi) says: “The gentleman possesses goodness, which he bequeaths to his descendants.” Worthy descendants are indeed a sovereign’s greatest blessing. Now the ritual impersonator responds to the ruler with such wishes for the worthiness of his descendants. Might he, too, have understood this?

“Heaven’s mandate descends and watches over those below; the common people inspire awe.”

Associate Examiner Yang, Assistant Instructor, comments: “The commentaries explain this topic most clearly, yet few writers can fully grasp it. [The transcription is unclear here: 文精人往, ?] They interpret it as Gaozong’s reverence for Heaven and fear of the people, entirely missing its original purport. In clarity of understanding and aptness of expression, no essay surpasses this one.”

Associate Examiner Zhu, Instructor, comments: “The topic means that Heaven’s mandate resides in the people, showing precisely why the people are to be feared. This essay apprehends the meaning clearly and expresses it neatly and lucidly. It has therefore been recorded as a model for later students.”

Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “This is precisely the meaning of the topic. No other essay surpasses it.”

Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “Classically elegant and worthy of selection.”

The poet, recognizing that Heaven’s mandate resides in the people, thus shows that the people are to be feared.

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
蓋民之視聽天命之所在也然則下民之勢不
亦為可畏哉宜詩人以是而頌美高宗也是詩
祀高宗之樂此則將言致中興之道而先言及
此謂夫彼蒼者天人皆以為高高在上穹然其
形而已殊不知天雖高也臨下有赫而命實降
監焉人皆以為赫赫在上蒼然其色而已殊不
知天雖遠也日監在茲而命實下視焉運乎奪
於冲漠之中視不自視而自民之視以為視是
其視在於民也宰去留於蒼冥之表聽不自聽
===
而自民之聽以為聽是其聽在於民也夫天雖
高而視聽有在乎民民雖卑而視聽有通乎天
吾知民心向背而天命之予奪繫之是民雖至
愚而有至神者存閭巷之喧騰一雷霆之震動
也嚴孰甚焉民心從違而天命之去留以之是
民雖至卑而有至高者寓億兆之觀瞻一日月
之照臨也嚴孰加焉是則下民有嚴如此則君
之不可不畏乎民也明矣高宗有見乎此而以
畏民為務此其所以得下民之心而受上天之
punctuated: 蓋民之視聽，天命之所在也。然則下民之勢，不亦為可畏哉？宜詩人以是而頌美高宗也。是詩，祀高宗之樂。此則將言致中興之道，而先言及此。謂夫彼蒼者天，人皆以為高高在上，穹然其形而已。殊不知天雖高也，臨下有赫，而命實降監焉。人皆以為赫赫在上，蒼然其色而已。殊不知天雖遠也，日監在茲，而命實下視焉。運乎奪於冲漠之中，視不自視，而自民之視以為視，是其視在於民也。宰去留於蒼冥之表，聽不自聽，而自民之聽以為聽，是其聽在於民也。夫天雖高，而視聽有在乎民；民雖卑，而視聽有通乎天。吾知民心向背，而天命之予奪繫之。是民雖至愚，而有至神者存；閭巷之喧騰，一雷霆之震動也，嚴孰甚焉？民心從違，而天命之去留以之。是民雖至卑，而有至高者寓；億兆之觀瞻，一日月之照臨也，嚴孰加焉？是則下民有嚴如此，則君之不可不畏乎民也明矣。高宗有見乎此，而以畏民為務，此其所以得下民之心而受上天之
translation_en:
…For what the people see and hear is where Heaven’s Mandate resides. Is not the power of the people below, then, something to be feared? It is fitting that the poet should praise Gaozong on this account. This ode was music for sacrifices to Gaozong. Here, before explaining the way by which he brought about a restoration, it first addresses this point. As for that azure Heaven, people all suppose that it is merely a vaulted shape high above. They fail to understand that, although Heaven is high, it looks down with blazing majesty, and its Mandate indeed descends to inspect what lies below. People all suppose that it is merely an azure color shining above. They fail to understand that, although Heaven is distant, it watches over us here each day, and its Mandate indeed looks down upon us. It governs bestowal and withdrawal [?] within silent, formless emptiness; it sees not through sight of its own, but takes the people’s sight as its sight. Thus its seeing resides in the people. It determines departure and continuance beyond the azure heavens; it hears not through hearing of its own, but takes the people’s hearing as its hearing. Thus its hearing resides in the people.

Although Heaven is high, its seeing and hearing reside in the people; although the people are lowly, their seeing and hearing communicate with Heaven. I know that the bestowal or withdrawal of Heaven’s Mandate depends upon whether the people’s hearts turn toward their ruler or away from him. Thus, although the people are utterly ignorant, something supremely numinous abides in them. The clamor of the lanes and alleys is the very shaking of thunder: what could be more awe-inspiring? The departure or continuance of Heaven’s Mandate follows whether the people’s hearts assent or resist. Thus, although the people are utterly lowly, something supremely exalted dwells in them. The gaze of the teeming multitudes is the very illumination of the sun and moon: what could surpass it in awe? Since the people below possess such awesome majesty, it is clear that the ruler must fear them. Gaozong perceived this and made fearing the people his concern. This is how he won the hearts of the people below and received from Heaven above its…

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
命也中興之福有由然哉大抵盤庚既沒治道
寖衰人心既離天命幾墜有商王業蕩乎其衰
矣一旦高宗者出惕然以撥亂反治為已任賞
無所僭刑無所濫畏民敬天之心不敢少怠合
人心於已離復天命於既墜此其所以平荊楚
畏諸侯而卒成中興之業也商之子孫可不知
所自哉
春秋
公及齊侯宋公陳侯衛侯鄭伯許男曹伯
會王世子于首止　諸侯盟于首止〔僖公五〕
年公會宰周公齊侯宋子衛侯鄭伯許男
曹伯于葵丘　諸侯盟于葵丘〔僖公九年〕
王藝
同考試官訓導陸　批〔此題作者雜用他傳多戾經旨惟此篇專主兩盟下胡傳而作非的見之學不能也是宜錄出〕
考試官教諭張　批〔深合尊重詞複之旨〕
考試官教諭李　批〔文有㢤越〕
===
春秋於霸主之會盟有複詞以美其正大倫者
punctuated:
命也。中興之福，有由然哉！大抵盤庚既沒，治道寖衰，人心既離，天命幾墜，有商王業蕩乎其衰矣。一旦高宗者出，惕然以撥亂反治為已任，賞無所僭，刑無所濫，畏民敬天之心不敢少怠，合人心於已離，復天命於既墜，此其所以平荊楚、畏諸侯，而卒成中興之業也。商之子孫，可不知所自哉？

春秋

公及齊侯、宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯，會王世子于首止。諸侯盟于首止。〔僖公五〕年，公會宰周公、齊侯、宋子、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯于葵丘。諸侯盟于葵丘。〔僖公九年〕

王藝

同考試官訓導陸，批〔此題作者雜用他傳，多戾經旨。惟此篇專主兩盟下胡傳而作，非的見之學不能也。是宜錄出。〕

考試官教諭張，批〔深合尊重詞複之旨。〕

考試官教諭李，批〔文有㢤越。〕

春秋於霸主之會盟，有複詞以美其正大倫者
translation_en:
…the mandate. Surely the blessings of restoration had their cause! Broadly speaking, after Pan Geng died, the way of good government gradually declined. The people's hearts became estranged, Heaven's mandate nearly fell away, and the royal enterprise of Shang tottered in decline. Then Gaozong arose, vigilantly taking upon himself the task of ending disorder and restoring good government. He bestowed no unwarranted rewards and imposed no excessive punishments. Never daring to relax his reverence for the people and respect for Heaven, he reunited the people's hearts after their estrangement and recovered Heaven's mandate after its fall. Thus he pacified Jing and Chu, inspired awe in the feudal lords, and finally accomplished the restoration. Could the descendants of Shang fail to recognize the source of this achievement?

Spring and Autumn Annals

“The duke, together with the marquis of Qi, the duke of Song, the marquis of Chen, the marquis of Wei, the earl of Zheng, the baron of Xu, and the earl of Cao, met the king's heir apparent at Shouzhi. The feudal lords made a covenant at Shouzhi.” 〔Fifth year of Duke Xi; the character for ‘year’ appears outside the annotation.〕 “The duke met the Grand Councilor, the duke of Zhou, the marquis of Qi, the viscount of Song, the marquis of Wei, the earl of Zheng, the baron of Xu, and the earl of Cao at Kuiqiu. The feudal lords made a covenant at Kuiqiu.” 〔Ninth year of Duke Xi.〕

Wang Yi

This essay alone bases its argument exclusively on Hu's commentary under the two covenants. Without learning grounded in accurate insight, this could not be accomplished. It therefore merits inclusion.〕

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
有複詞以美其明大禁者此見齊桓有大功於
天下也春秋複詞書之良有以夫慨周道不復
於西鎬幸齊桓主霸於東州于時惠王寵帶子
鄭危疑天下之大倫殆襃矣桓公有憂之於是
控大扶小因世子下臨既會首止以商同尊之
謀及世子返駕復盟首止以申翼戴之義定大
本於杌隉而國勢不搖奠神器於靈長而邦家
有慶未幾太子踐祚是為襄王一舉而父子君
臣之道皆得焉桓之功何如其大哉吾知冠裳
===
無左衽之憂人類免禽犢之患未必不賴於此
也仲尼稱其一匡豈無謂乎故春秋於會盟同
地再言首止所以著其美之大而不厭於繁也
于時襄王始政諸侯放恣天子之大禁久廢矣
桓公欲明之於是率與協同因宰孔賜胙既會
葵丘以展下拜之恭逮宰孔言旋復盟葵丘以
嚴約束之令初命一詞三綱之典攸係四命迭
舉九經之要具存已而牲血不歃信在諸侯一
舉而文武成康之法復振焉桓之功又何如其
punctuated:
有複詞以美其明大禁者，此見齊桓有大功於天下也。《春秋》複詞書之，良有以夫！慨周道不復於西鎬，幸齊桓主霸於東州。于時惠王寵帶，子鄭危疑，天下之大倫殆襃矣。桓公有憂之，於是控大扶小，因世子下臨，既會首止以商同尊之謀；及世子返駕，復盟首止以申翼戴之義。定大本於杌隉，而國勢不搖；奠神器於靈長，而邦家有慶。未幾，太子踐祚，是為襄王。一舉而父子君臣之道皆得焉，桓之功何如其大哉！吾知冠裳無左衽之憂，人類免禽犢之患，未必不賴於此也。仲尼稱其一匡，豈無謂乎？故《春秋》於會盟同地，再言首止，所以著其美之大，而不厭於繁也。
于時襄王始政，諸侯放恣，天子之大禁久廢矣。桓公欲明之，於是率與協同，因宰孔賜胙，既會葵丘以展下拜之恭；逮宰孔言旋，復盟葵丘以嚴約束之令。初命一詞，三綱之典攸係；四命迭舉，九經之要具存。已而牲血不歃，信在諸侯。一舉而文武成康之法復振焉，桓之功又何如其
translation_en:
…and there are repeated phrases that praise his clarification of the great prohibitions. This shows that Duke Huan of Qi rendered great service to all under Heaven. There was indeed good reason for the Spring and Autumn Annals to record these events with repeated wording! It was lamentable that the Way of Zhou had not been restored at western Hao, but fortunate that Duke Huan of Qi exercised leadership as hegemon in the eastern region. At that time, King Hui favored Dai, and the position of his son Zheng was precarious and uncertain. The great human relationships throughout the realm were nearly in decline [?]. Duke Huan was concerned about this. Accordingly, he restrained the powerful and supported the weak. Taking advantage of the royal heir’s visit, he first assembled the lords at Shouzhi to discuss a plan for jointly honoring him. When the heir’s carriage had departed, he then concluded a covenant at Shouzhi to reaffirm their duty to support him. He secured the great foundation amid peril, so that the stability of the state was not shaken; he established the sacred vessel of sovereignty on an enduring footing, bringing blessings to the royal house. Before long, the heir ascended the throne as King Xiang. Through a single undertaking, the proper relationships of father and son, ruler and subject were both secured. How great was Duke Huan’s achievement! I know that those wearing ceremonial caps and robes had no fear of having to fasten their garments on the left in the manner of barbarians, and humankind escaped the danger of becoming like birds and calves [?]; this may well have depended upon that achievement. When Zhongni praised him for setting the realm right in one stroke, could his words have been without meaning? Thus, although the assembly and covenant took place at the same location, the Spring and Autumn Annals names Shouzhi twice, displaying the greatness of his merit without shunning repetition.
At that time, King Xiang had just begun his reign, and the regional lords acted without restraint. The Son of Heaven’s great prohibitions had long fallen into disuse. Duke Huan wished to make them clear. Accordingly, he led the participating lords in concerted action. On the occasion when Minister Kong bestowed sacrificial meat, he first assembled them at Kuiqiu to display his reverence by bowing below the hall. Once Minister Kong had departed on his return journey, he concluded a covenant at Kuiqiu to make its binding injunctions strict. The wording of the first injunction bore upon the principles of the Three Bonds; the four further injunctions, set forth in succession, embodied all the essentials of the Nine Guiding Principles of government. Then, without smearing their lips with the sacrificial animal’s blood, the regional lords established mutual trust. Through a single undertaking, the institutions of Kings Wen, Wu, Cheng, and Kang were revived. How great, again, was Duke Huan’s…

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
大哉吾知收人心於星散之餘扶王綱於解紐
之後未必不伏於此也孟子與其爲盛豈無見
乎故春秋於會盟同地再言葵丘又以著其美
之大而不嫌於贅也吁始也一舉而大倫正終
也一舉而大禁明桓亦當時之傑然者歟雖然
桓之霸事可謂盛矣何葵丘一盛而遽衰歟蓋
桓之霸仲之相也桓無至誠之德仲無格心之
學志之所期者霸也非王也期於王者至於王
期於霸者止於霸桓仲之願既滿於葵丘之盛
桓仲之業不得不衰於葵丘之盟也使桓仲以
王道自期其功烈豈止於葵丘邪豈衰於葵丘
邪
===
西狩獲麟　〔哀公十四年〕
袁擯
同考試官訓導陸　批　〔題本正大作者類多不諳傳意〕
〔此篇陳文此作前用王道人倫說後用孟子性命之言斷化出終天〕
〔道之意篇末又斷制獲麟之疑他日澤用經學必能處大事矣〕
〔疑矣末房之白月末難然〕
punctuated:
大哉！吾知收人心於星散之餘，扶王綱於解紐之後，未必不伏於此也。孟子與其爲盛，豈無見乎？故春秋於會盟同地，再言葵丘，又以著其美之大，而不嫌於贅也。吁！始也一舉而大倫正，終也一舉而大禁明，桓亦當時之傑然者歟！雖然，桓之霸事可謂盛矣，何葵丘一盛而遽衰歟？蓋桓之霸，仲之相也。桓無至誠之德，仲無格心之學，志之所期者霸也，非王也。期於王者至於王，期於霸者止於霸。桓仲之願既滿於葵丘之盛，桓仲之業不得不衰於葵丘之盟也。使桓仲以王道自期，其功烈豈止於葵丘邪？豈衰於葵丘邪？

西狩獲麟。〔哀公十四年〕
袁擯
同考試官訓導陸，批：〔題本正大，作者類多不諳傳意。〕〔此篇陳文此作，前用王道人倫說，後用孟子性命之言斷，化出終天〕〔道之意。篇末又斷制獲麟之疑，他日澤用經學，必能處大事矣。〕〔疑矣，末房之白月末難然。〕
translation_en:
…great indeed! I know that the means of gathering people’s hearts after they had scattered like stars, and of sustaining the bonds of royal authority after they had come undone, may well have lain within this. When Mencius approved it as a flourishing achievement, was this not based on insight? Thus, although the meeting and covenant took place at the same location, the Spring and Autumn Annals names Kuiqiu twice, again to display the greatness of the achievement, without regarding the repetition as superfluous. Ah! At the outset, a single action set the cardinal human relationships right; at the conclusion, a single action made the great prohibitions clear. Was Duke Huan not an outstanding figure of his age?

Nevertheless, although Duke Huan’s achievements as hegemon may be called flourishing, why did they suddenly decline after reaching their height at Kuiqiu? Duke Huan’s hegemony depended on Guan Zhong’s service as his minister. Huan lacked the virtue of utmost sincerity, and Zhong lacked the learning needed to rectify his ruler’s heart. Their ambition was hegemony, not true kingship. Those who aspire to true kingship attain it; those who aspire to hegemony stop at hegemony. Once the aspirations of Huan and Zhong had been fulfilled in the glory of Kuiqiu, their enterprise inevitably began to decline with the covenant there. Had Huan and Zhong set their sights on the Kingly Way, would their achievements have stopped at Kuiqiu? Would they have declined at Kuiqiu?

“On a hunt in the west, a qilin was captured.” 〔Fourteenth year of Duke Ai.〕
Yuan Bin 袁擯

Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Assistant Instructor: 〔The topic is fundamentally upright and weighty, but most writers do not understand the meaning of the commentary.〕 〔This essay’s presentation [?] first employs an explanation of the Kingly Way and human relationships, then draws its conclusion from Mencius’s words on human nature and destiny, developing from these the idea of bringing the text to a close in accordance with the Way of Heaven.〕 〔At the end, the essay also resolves doubts about the capture of the qilin [?]. If in future the author applies his classical learning in office [?], he will surely be able to handle great affairs.〕 〔The final annotation is garbled: “doubt,” “last examination room,” “white moon,” and “difficult … so” are discernible [?].〕

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭張　批〔講出絕筆於天道之意逈異〕
〔衆作〕
考試官教諭李　批〔深得胡傳之旨〕
聖經有感乎天道聖筆因終乎天道此西狩獲
麟有以見聖人秉筆之成功絕筆之妙用也且
麟之為瑞也昭昭矣非盛世不出非明王不至
春秋何世也魯哀何君也麟何為獲於魯之西
狩乎蓋天地間之常理惟感與應爾人事感於
下則天道應於上世值周末彝倫之壞甚矣夫
===
子為世道之計作春秋之書明王道以垂範百
王正人倫以綱維百世治功與禹周相配神化
與天地同流志氣交孚而天人之相感深矣故
制作之文方成於衆魯帝王之瑞遂出於西郊
是豈偶然者哉正與河洛之呈祥鳳鳥之來儀
同一感應之理也然則何為絕筆於獲麟乎蓋
聖人之於天道曰命與性爾命固由於天而性
則在於己世值周末天道之否極矣夫子致盡
性之功任參贊之責以人合天而不任於天以
punctuated:
考試官教諭張批〔講出絕筆於天道之意，逈異衆作〕。
考試官教諭李批〔深得胡傳之旨〕。
聖經有感乎天道，聖筆因終乎天道。此西狩獲麟，有以見聖人秉筆之成功、絕筆之妙用也。且麟之為瑞也昭昭矣，非盛世不出，非明王不至。春秋何世也？魯哀何君也？麟何為獲於魯之西狩乎？蓋天地間之常理，惟感與應爾。人事感於下，則天道應於上。世值周末，彝倫之壞甚矣。夫子為世道之計，作春秋之書，明王道以垂範百王，正人倫以綱維百世。治功與禹周相配，神化與天地同流，志氣交孚，而天人之相感深矣。故制作之文方成於衆魯，帝王之瑞遂出於西郊。是豈偶然者哉？正與河洛之呈祥、鳳鳥之來儀，同一感應之理也。然則何為絕筆於獲麟乎？蓋聖人之於天道，曰命與性爾。命固由於天，而性則在於己。世值周末，天道之否極矣。夫子致盡性之功，任參贊之責，以人合天而不任於天，以
translation_en:
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: 〔The explanation of why the writing ends with the Way of Heaven is markedly different from the other compositions.〕
Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: 〔This grasps profoundly the purport of Hu’s Commentary.〕
The sage’s classic elicits a response from the Way of Heaven, and the sage’s brush therefore concludes with the Way of Heaven. The capture of the qilin during the hunt in the west thus reveals the sage’s accomplished work in taking up his brush and the subtle efficacy of laying it down. That the qilin is an auspicious sign is perfectly clear: it does not appear except in a flourishing age, nor arrive except under an enlightened king. What sort of age was the Spring and Autumn period? What sort of ruler was Duke Ai of Lu? Why was a qilin captured during Lu’s hunt in the west? The constant principle operating between Heaven and Earth is simply that of stimulus and response. When human affairs provide the stimulus below, the Way of Heaven responds above. In the declining years of Zhou, the enduring human relationships had fallen into grave disorder. Planning for the moral order of the world, the Master composed the Spring and Autumn Annals. He clarified the kingly Way to set a pattern for a hundred kings, and rectified human relationships to provide a governing framework for a hundred generations. His achievements in bringing order matched those of Yu and the Duke of Zhou; his wondrous transforming influence flowed together with Heaven and Earth. Purpose and vital force resonated with one another, and the mutual responsiveness of Heaven and humanity was profound. Thus, just as his composition was completed in Lu [?], an auspicious sign of imperial kingship appeared in the western outskirts. Could this have been accidental? It exemplified precisely the same principle of stimulus and response as the auspicious signs presented by the Yellow and Luo Rivers and the phoenix’s coming in stately bearing.
Why, then, did he lay down his brush at the capture of the qilin? The sage’s relation to the Way of Heaven concerns simply destiny and nature. Destiny indeed comes from Heaven, whereas one’s nature resides within oneself. In the declining years of Zhou, the obstruction of the Way of Heaven had reached its extreme. The Master accomplished the work of fully realizing his nature and assumed responsibility for participating in and assisting the transforming work of Heaven and Earth. Through human effort he brought humanity into accord with Heaven, without leaving matters to Heaven; through …

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
義立命而不委於命至誠格天地之心瑞應兆
文明之治天人脗合而聖人之能事畢矣故經
以人事而作因以天道而終是豈茍然者哉正
與周南之麟趾召南之騶虞同一終篇之義也
秉筆也而天道應絕筆也以天道終聖人先天
而天弗違後天而奉天時其功用之極有如此
夫雖然獲麟之說不一曰文成致麟曰感麟而
作要皆未可知也孟子曰孔子懼作春秋此其
大者麟固為聖人出也然春秋之作不係於麟
===
之有無麟不出春秋未必不作也春秋不作麟
未必不出也特以麟而終其所感深矣此固獲
麟意也
禮記
凡居民財必因天地寒煖燥濕廣谷大川
異制民生其閒異俗剛柔輕重遲速異齊
五味異和器械異制衣服異宜脩其教不
易其俗齊其政不易其宜
田登
punctuated:
義立命而不委於命，至誠格天地之心，瑞應兆文明之治，天人脗合而聖人之能事畢矣。故經以人事而作，因以天道而終，是豈茍然者哉？正與《周南》之《麟趾》、《召南》之《騶虞》同一終篇之義也。秉筆也而天道應，絕筆也以天道終。聖人先天而天弗違，後天而奉天時，其功用之極有如此夫！雖然，獲麟之說不一，曰文成致麟，曰感麟而作，要皆未可知也。孟子曰：「孔子懼，作《春秋》。」此其大者。麟固為聖人出也，然《春秋》之作不係於麟之有無。麟不出，《春秋》未必不作也；《春秋》不作，麟未必不出也。特以麟而終，其所感深矣。此固獲麟意也。

禮記

凡居民財，必因天地寒煖燥濕，廣谷大川異制，民生其閒異俗，剛柔輕重遲速異齊，五味異和，器械異制，衣服異宜。脩其教，不易其俗；齊其政，不易其宜。

田登
translation_en:
…through righteousness he establishes his destiny without abandoning himself to it. His utmost sincerity moves the heart of Heaven and Earth; an auspicious response heralds a reign of cultured enlightenment. Heaven and humanity accord, and the sage’s work is complete. Thus the Classic was composed to address human affairs and concluded in accordance with the Way of Heaven. Could this have been arbitrary? Its conclusion has precisely the same significance as “The Qilin’s Hooves” at the end of the “Airs of Zhou and the South” and “The Zouyu” at the end of the “Airs of Shao and the South.” When he took up his brush, the Way of Heaven responded; when he laid it down, he concluded in accordance with the Way of Heaven. When the sage acts before Heaven, Heaven does not oppose him; when he acts after Heaven, he follows Heaven’s seasons. Such is the supreme efficacy of his work!

Nevertheless, explanations of the capture of the qilin differ. Some say that the completion of the text brought the qilin; others, that he was moved by the qilin to compose it. Ultimately, neither claim can be established. Mengzi said, “Confucius grew fearful and composed the Spring and Autumn Annals.” This is the essential point. The qilin certainly appeared for the sage, yet the composition of the Spring and Autumn Annals did not depend on whether it appeared. Had the qilin not appeared, the Annals might still have been composed; had the Annals not been composed, the qilin might still have appeared. Yet he chose to conclude with the qilin, so profoundly was he moved by it. This, surely, is the significance of the capture of the qilin.

Record of Rites

“In settling the people and managing their resources [?], one must take account of Heaven and Earth: cold and warmth, dryness and dampness. Broad valleys and great rivers differ in their configuration, and the people born among them differ in their customs. Their dispositions differ in firmness and gentleness, lightness and gravity, slowness and quickness. They blend the five flavors differently, fashion their implements differently, and find different clothing suitable. Refine their instruction without changing their customs; bring their governance into order without changing what suits them.”

Tian Deng.

When the sage kings stored up supplies for the people’s use, they did not force uniformity upon things difficult to make uniform; they unified only what could be unified. Customs are rooted in human feelings and therefore cannot be made uniform, whereas government and instruction originate in Heaven-endowed nature and can be made uniform. Could the sage kings, in dealing with these matters, fail to judge what was practicable and what was not, and accordingly shape and assist them? The chapter “Royal Regulations” records this, meaning that the people’s daily lives necessarily require material resources, and that the sage kings necessarily had a proper way of storing them. Why is this so?
Thus, in the climatic influences of Heaven and Earth, the southeast is generally warm and the northwest generally cold. Accordingly, fine hemp garments and fur robes are made to meet the needs of cold and warmth. High ground is necessarily dry and low ground necessarily wet. Accordingly, boats and carriages are made to meet the needs of dry and wet terrain. Valleys are broad and extensive; rivers flow and are great. Ever since Heaven and Earth first separated, their physical configurations have differed. People live in valleys and along rivers; ever since the two primal powers took their places, their customs too have differed. As regards the mildness or urgency of their dispositions, there are differing degrees of firmness and gentleness, lightness and gravity, slowness and quickness. As regards the seasoning of food and drink, there are different blends of saltiness, bitterness, sourness, pungency, sweetness, and smoothness. Implements all serve to meet practical needs, yet their designs inevitably differ in some respects. Clothing likewise serves to adorn the body, yet what is appropriate in dress does not…

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
能無或異聖王於此亦豈必強之使同哉惟脩
其三綱五典之教使彝倫攸敘典禮克敦陶民
性於治化之中而已爾若夫民情之異俗曷嘗
有所更張乎齊其禮樂刑政之用俾紀綱振舉
法度脩明蕭民心於矩度之內而已爾若夫民
俗之異宜何嘗有所變易乎是知同其政教則
有以復人性之本然因其俗宜則有以順人情
之自然聖王財成輔相之道何以加於此哉嗟
夫天生材以資世民須材以養生民材之當居
===
也尚矣柰何五方皆有性千里不同風欲一律
以齊之未必不咈其情之所安故聖王之馭世
必因其俗宜之異而一以政教之同則民材以
備民用以足不強其必齊而自無不齊不強其
必得而自無不得此其所以善於調劑天下而
致大一統之治也歟
脩身及家平均天下
邊貢

punctuated:
能無或異。聖王於此，亦豈必強之使同哉？惟脩其三綱五典之教，使彝倫攸敘，典禮克敦，陶民性於治化之中而已爾。若夫民情之異俗，曷嘗有所更張乎？齊其禮樂刑政之用，俾紀綱振舉，法度脩明，蕭民心於矩度之內而已爾。若夫民俗之異宜，何嘗有所變易乎？是知同其政教，則有以復人性之本然；因其俗宜，則有以順人情之自然。聖王財成輔相之道，何以加於此哉？嗟夫！天生材以資世，民須材以養生，民材之當居也尚矣。柰何五方皆有性，千里不同風，欲一律以齊之，未必不咈其情之所安。故聖王之馭世，必因其俗宜之異，而一以政教之同，則民材以備，民用以足。不強其必齊，而自無不齊；不強其必得，而自無不得。此其所以善於調劑天下，而致大一統之治也歟？

脩身及家，平均天下。
邊貢。

translation_en:
…cannot be without differences. In these matters, would the sage kings insist on forcing people to be alike? They merely cultivated instruction in the Three Bonds and Five Constant Relationships, so that the enduring human relationships were duly ordered and the prescribed rites faithfully observed, molding the people's dispositions through good government and moral transformation. As for the differing customs expressive of people's inclinations, when did they ever alter them? They made uniform the application of rites, music, punishments, and government, so that the guiding principles were upheld and laws and standards were maintained and clarified, bringing the people's hearts within established bounds [?]. As for the differing practices appropriate to local customs, when did they ever change them? Thus we know that uniform government and teaching can restore human nature to its original condition, while accommodation to local customs and circumstances can accord with the natural inclinations of human feeling. How could anything surpass this way of the sage kings, who shaped and assisted the workings of Heaven and Earth? Alas! Heaven produces materials to supply the world, and the people depend on materials to sustain life. The proper placement of people and materials has long been important. Yet each of the five regions has its own character, and customs differ across a thousand li. If one seeks to make them uniform by a single standard, one may well run counter to what people find congenial. Thus, in governing the world, the sage kings necessarily accommodated differences in local customs and circumstances while unifying them through common government and teaching. Materials for the people were thereby fully provided, and their needs adequately supplied. Without forcing uniformity, nothing failed to be brought into order; without forcing attainment, nothing failed to find its proper place. Was this not how they skillfully harmonized all under Heaven and achieved the governance of a grand, unified realm?

Cultivating oneself, extending this to the family, and bringing equity and order to all under Heaven.
Bian Gong.

…Most neglect the meaning of the commentary, generally dividing the topic at the points concerning cultivating oneself and ordering the family—a thoroughly pointless approach. This composition alone develops its argument in accordance with the received commentary and annotations, grasping the essential meaning profoundly. Moreover, it is clear and forceful, with thoroughly well-ordered prose. I therefore selected it as the best essay in this examining room.
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: It explains how understanding music makes clear the way to cultivate oneself. Worth selecting.
Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: It integrates the meaning of the commentary into a coherent composition. Selected.
When the gentleman understands ancient music and thereby rectifies his foundation, his transforming influence extends to those both far and near. For the self is the foundation of the family, the state, and all under Heaven. If he can rectify that foundation and then extend and apply this, where would his transforming influence fail to reach? Formerly, because Marquis Wen of Wei did not understand what made ancient music worthy of delight, Zixia explained matters to him in these terms. His meaning was that all under Heaven, the state, and the family are rooted in the self, while cultivation of the self is rooted in music. If the gentleman truly understands the harmony and correctness of ancient music—expansive without becoming unrestrained, with its ensemble, observance, tapping, and drumming proceeding in due order [?]—he will discern the principles of harmony and order down to their finest details. If he understands how ancient music begins with the civil dance, rooted in benevolence, and concludes with the martial dance, regulated by righteousness, the Way of benevolence and righteousness will shine clearly in its minutest particulars. When he uses this to cultivate himself, I see his desires calmed, his hearing and sight keen, and his dross dissolved; his agitation released, his vital energies harmonious and tranquil, and his corrupt impurities swept away. Is not the self thereby cultivated? Once the way of cultivating oneself is understood, he strengthens his care for those nearby and extends it to those far away, so that his transforming influence reaches everywhere. Thus the self is the foundation of the family. When he uses this to order the family, music is practiced and human relationships become clearly defined: fathers and sons are harmonious and affectionate, elders and juniors harmonious and deferential. A reverent and harmonious transforming influence manifests itself within the household, and licentiousness and perversity do not arise. The way of concord is strengthened throughout the nine degrees of kinship, and discord does not emerge. Is not the family thereby…

title: 弘治八年山東鄉試錄
text:
而齊乎家者一國天下之本也以之平均天下
則樂行而民向方風焉以移俗焉以易世躋泰
和無偏無黨上下一德也民囿熈皡無反無側
遠近同化也天下不於是而平均乎吁君子知
古樂而明脩身之道則家齊國治而天下平如
此吾君之聽樂烏可不知所擇耶抑論古樂之
為用大矣時至春秋樂教不興民偽日滋當時
之人靡然趨於新樂之是好求其知古樂之正
而好之者幾何人哉無怪乎魏文侯聽之而惟
恐卧也向非子夏歷舉而詳告之則人又孰從
而知古樂之正足以脩身及家平均天下也哉
善乎吾夫子論為邦有曰樂則韶舞放鄭聲子
夏之言其有得於此歟
===
第貳塲
論
君子之學以潤身為本
同考試官教諭鄧　批　作論當以意為主造語
杜　珏
punctuated:
而齊乎？家者，一國天下之本也。以之平均天下，則樂行而民向方，風焉以移，俗焉以易，世躋泰和，無偏無黨，上下一德也；民囿熈皡，無反無側，遠近同化也。天下不於是而平均乎？吁！君子知古樂而明脩身之道，則家齊國治而天下平如此，吾君之聽樂，烏可不知所擇耶？抑論古樂之為用大矣！時至春秋，樂教不興，民偽日滋。當時之人靡然趨於新樂之是好，求其知古樂之正而好之者，幾何人哉？無怪乎魏文侯聽之而惟恐卧也。向非子夏歷舉而詳告之，則人又孰從而知古樂之正足以脩身及家、平均天下也哉？善乎！吾夫子論為邦有曰：「樂則韶舞，放鄭聲。」子夏之言，其有得於此歟？

第貳塲

論

君子之學以潤身為本

translation_en:
…and thereby be brought into order? The family is the foundation of the state and of all under Heaven. By using ancient music to bring equity and order to all under Heaven, music will prevail and the people will turn toward righteousness. Manners will be transformed and customs changed; the age will attain great harmony. Without partiality or faction, those above and below will share one virtue. The people will dwell in radiant peace; without perversity or deviation, those far and near will be transformed alike. Will all under Heaven not thereby be brought into equity and order? Ah! When the gentleman understands ancient music and comprehends the way of cultivating himself, his family is ordered, the state is governed, and all under Heaven is thus brought to peace. How could our ruler, in listening to music, fail to know what to choose?

Indeed, the efficacy of ancient music is great! By the Spring and Autumn period, instruction through music no longer flourished, and deceit among the people increased daily. People of that time followed the prevailing current, delighting only in new music. How many could be found who understood the rectitude of ancient music and delighted in it? No wonder Marquis Wen of Wei feared only that he would fall asleep when listening to it. Had Zixia not enumerated its features and explained them in detail, from whom could people have learned that the rectitude of ancient music suffices to cultivate oneself, extend that cultivation to the family, and bring equity and order to all under Heaven? How excellent were our Master's words on governing a state: “For music, use the Shao dance; banish the sounds of Zheng.” Had Zixia's words perhaps drawn their insight from this?
